name: Chisel
text:
I think we should start by creating a comprehensive inventory of all links, without prioritizing any at this stage. This decision allows us to get a complete picture of what we're dealing with, which is essential for making informed choices later on. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially spending more time upfront on cataloging, but this approach reduces the risk of overlooking important links or misjudging their importance, as Scriv pointed out. This foundation will ultimately help us make better decisions and ensure we're pushing towards 100% link coverage efficiently.

name: Sift
text: I'm not convinced that ignoring priorities altogether is the best approach, Scriv - the real risk is spreading ourselves too thin and making minimal progress on any front. A better alternative might be to conduct a quick, high-level assessment to identify the most critical links, and then validate those assumptions through data or user feedback. What would settle this argument is some concrete data on link usage patterns, which would help us understand where to focus our efforts and make more informed decisions.

name: Scope
text: I think we should create a simple categorization system to group links into three tiers: high, medium, and low priority. This decision allows us to focus on the most critical links first, while still acknowledging the importance of the others, and it's the best option because it gives us a clear direction without requiring a comprehensive inventory that might delay our progress. By doing so, we're accepting the trade-off of potentially overlooking some nuances in the links that don't fit neatly into our categorization system. This approach will enable us to make tangible progress toward our goal of pushing link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: The risk isn’t just wrong assumptions—it’s that we’ll *never know* we’re wrong until we’ve wasted days chasing the wrong links. Instead, let’s lock in a simple, verifiable rule: every link gets a one-sentence justification for its priority tier, written down *before* we touch it. If two people can’t agree on why a link matters, it defaults to the lowest tier. That’s not slower—it’s the only way to avoid rework when we realize we’ve been optimizing for noise.
